body: Her bedroom is quiet and she cannot work in it, so a girl of fifteen has her homework spread across one end of the kitchen table at ten past six, with the extractor fan running and making this the loudest room in the house. Her mother has her back turned and is doing something to an onion. Somewhere between the onion and the second question about oxbow lakes, the girl says, to the tabletop rather than to anybody, that she does not think she has any friends this year. Her mother does not turn round. She says that is a rotten way to feel, and asks whether she wants the cheese in this. The girl says yes.
That sentence was never going to be said in a quiet room. It needed a fan, a knife, an onion and a mother whose back was turned. It needed cover.

Sanctuary has drifted into meaning the large room with the good acoustics, which is a shame, because the older sense is far more useful to anybody who does not happen to have one. A sanctuary is a place where something is protected — where a thing that can be got at everywhere else cannot be reached.

It is worth taking the word at its legal weight rather than its architectural one. For centuries sanctuary named a hard practical fact: a man who reached the church could not be taken out of it. What made that work was not the height of the roof or the quality of the singing. It was a line on the ground and a general agreement about what could not cross it. The load-bearing part was always the boundary, and the promise attached to it, which is why the word survives in the phrase we still use about wildlife: a sanctuary is where the thing that is hunted elsewhere is not hunted here.

By that definition a kitchen qualifies rather more often than a building does. 46 frequencies on this dial run day and night, and the hour that concerns this article is the ordinary one between five and seven in the evening, when most of what a family will ever say to each other actually gets said.

Running a room that way costs something specific. It costs the right to use what you hear. A parent who is told the true version of how a day went, and who produces it three weeks later in an argument as evidence, has closed the room permanently, and no amount of warmth will reopen it. That is the whole discipline and it is harder than it sounds, because the true version is often exactly the thing you most want to bring up. A sanctuary is not a quiet room. It is a place where a particular thing is safe, and quiet is optional.

Rooms of that kind have become scarce, and the reason is not that families have got colder. It is that almost nothing said anywhere now stays where it was said. A remark made at fourteen can be produced at nineteen, in the original spelling. This is the first generation to grow up with a permanent record of its own worst afternoons, and the effect is not that they say less — it is that they get very good at saying the version that is safe to keep. A room with no record in it has become an unusual amenity, and most households own one without realising what they have.

The physical arrangement does more of the work than anybody credits. Nobody sits at the head of a kitchen; there is usually no head. Hands are busy, so silences are not awkward, and eyes have a legitimate place to go. People pass through, which means anybody can leave without it meaning that they left. Nothing is scheduled, so nothing has to be concluded. It is, structurally, the opposite of a meeting, and the skill it teaches — talking to somebody who is not looking at you — is one that most of the difficult sentences in a family require.
Which is why the good conversation almost never happens where it was arranged to happen.

The sit-down deserves its due, and some things genuinely need it — a decision, an apology, a piece of news that cannot be delivered sideways. But the sit-down has one property it cannot lose: it announces itself. The moment a person is told that we need to talk, they arrive prepared, and what arrives with them is the presentable account. You will get a truthful conversation. You will very rarely get the sentence that was not going to be said.
A room that demands attention will only ever be told what a person has already decided to say.

There is a boy of eleven from two doors down who does his homework at that same table on Wednesdays, because there is nobody in at his house until seven. It began as an arrangement between mothers and nobody has revisited it in two years. He is laid a place without discussion. He does not talk much, he eats an enormous amount, and he is the only person at that table who ever says thank you for the dinner. Once, in October, he asked whether it was all right to not like somebody you are supposed to like. He got an answer, and then the plates went in the sink, and it has never been mentioned since.

That is the mechanism, and it is unglamorous. He was not counselled, invited or drawn out. He was in a room where the cost of saying a true thing was low, at an hour when the adults had their hands full.

A kitchen makes a poor sanctuary in several obvious ways and they should be admitted. There is no privacy in it. The wrong sibling overhears the thing that was not for them. A house with a bad temperature has it worst in the kitchen, because that is where the tired people collide, and calling such a room protected would be a lie. Music can make it worse as easily as better: a radio can be a way of never letting a silence last long enough for anybody to fill it,

Even so, the interruptions are not the flaw in this room. They are what makes it usable. A hard sentence can be started in a kitchen because it can be abandoned in a kitchen — somebody comes in for a glass, and the subject is dropped, and nobody has failed at anything. In a room built for the conversation, a half-said thing becomes a commitment, and everybody knows it, which is precisely why the half-said thing never gets started there. What looks like a lack of seriousness is the escape route, and people will only walk towards a difficult thing when they can see one.

So the useful version of the word is not architectural. A sanctuary is a room with a boundary and a promise: inside it, honesty is not hunted. The kitchen qualifies because it is where the family actually assembles, where the difficult conversation eventually gets had, and where a child learns what the adults are really like by watching how they behave when they are tired. The protected thing is not silence — it is the assumption that a person can say the true version of their day without it being used against them later.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 frequencies, 46 of them on air. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, gospel, country, hymns, ambient and a good deal more. Some frequencies carry teaching and prayer, and some are built for children. 40 are international, hosted in 29 languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards. For the purpose described here, the question is narrower than usual: what can play in a kitchen for two hours without ever once asking to be attended to?

Start at HM 310.90 — Latin Worship. It is Santiago Inspire’s catalogue, Latin ballad and cumbia and samba and theatrical-liturgical writing, sung in English, and the evening programme is Latin Worship Nights. It is recommended here for a reason that has little to do with the language. It is music out of cultures where the kitchen is the room — where the cooking, the arguing, the singing and the praying all happen at one table, and where nobody has ever confused a quiet room with a holy one. It is warm, it is unembarrassed, and it does not ask to be attended to. Put it on at five and it will not lower the volume of your house. It will lower the temperature of it, which is a different thing, and the one this article has been after.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is already on the worktop and press play. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have, and you can add the page to a home screen if you want it nearer. Do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are really reaching for at which hours — which is how the next one gets built.

So try this rather than resolving anything. Put HM 310.90 on at about five, before anybody is home, and leave it low enough that nobody has to talk over it. Cook something that needs your hands. Do not turn round. Give it a fortnight of ordinary evenings and see what gets said to the tabletop in a room where nobody was being asked anything at all.
